cognate: Gk ὠμός = Ved. āmá- (*h₂eh₃mó- 'raw'); Gk κρέας = Ved. kravís- (*kréwh₂s 'raw flesh'); Gk ἔδω/ἔδμεναι = Ved. ad- (*h₁ed- 'eat') in the Homeric and Atharvan witnesses
drift_or_renewal: the 'human' qualifier is renewed in each branch with a derivative of the local word for man (Gk ἀνθρώπων gen., Hom. ἀνδρόμεα; Ved. pauruṣeya- from púruṣa-); AV also renews the generic flesh word in the first member (māṃsam), keeping kravís- for the second
shared_syntax: adjective 'raw' + flesh-noun (RV āmásya kravíṣaḥ; Hom. ὤμ' … κρέα), and the paired phrases 'raw [flesh]' + 'human flesh' as objects of 'eat': AVŚ 8.6 āmaṃ māṃsam adanti … pauruṣeyaṃ … kraviḥ ~ Arist. ὠμοῖς … ἀνθρώπων κρέασιν; in the Aristotle pivot ὠμοῖς and κρέασιν are parallel members (raw [sc. flesh] vs human flesh), not a single syntagm
context: Eating raw and human flesh marks the inhuman: Aristotle's 'bestial' peoples of the Pontus (ὠμοῖς … ἀνθρώπων κρέασιν); the AV's flesh-eating demons who eat raw flesh and human flesh (āmaṃ … adanti … pauruṣeyaṃ … kraviḥ; cf. āma adaḥ kravya adaḥ AVP 1.42, āmā́daḥ RV 10.87.7); RV 10.87.16 the sorcerer smeared with human flesh (paúruṣeyeṇa kravíṣā); Homer's Achilles wishing to eat Hector raw (ὤμ' … κρέα ἔδμεναι Il. 22.347) and the Cyclops eating human flesh (ἀνδρόμεα κρέ' ἔδων Od. 9.297). The direct adjective+noun witness in the RV (āmásya kravíṣaḥ 1.162.10) is however sacrificial, the smell of the raw flesh of the sacrificed horse (cf. áśvasya kravíṣaḥ 1.162.9), not savage. κρέας + ὠμός co-occur in Homer only once, in the cannibal wish, and kravís- is rare in the RV (3x: horse sacrifice 2x, human flesh 1x), so the match is a specialised archaic collocation rather than everyday food vocabulary; the demon/cannibal framing rests on AVŚ 8.6, RV 10.87, Il. 22.347, Od. 9.297.
phrase: *h₂eh₃mó- *kréwh₂s *h₁ed- 'eat raw flesh' / 'eat human flesh' (mark of beast, demon, cannibal)

cognate: Gk μέλι(τ-) = Lat. mel (*mélit 'honey'); Gk γλυκύς = Lat. dulcis (*dl̥kú-/*dléwkus 'sweet')
drift_or_renewal: Vedic keeps the comparative figure but renews both lexemes: mádhu- (cognate with μέθυ, not μέλι) and svādú- (cognate with ἡδύς/suāuis, not γλυκύς): AVP 19.29 svādoś … svādīyāṃsaṃ madhoś … madhumattaram
shared_syntax: comparative of 'sweet' with 'honey' as standard of comparison: Hom. μέλιτος γλυκίων (gen. of comparison) ~ Pl. melle dulci dulcior (abl. of comparison); plus attributive 'sweet honey' (Arist. μέλι … γλυκύ; Lucr. dulci … melle; Hom. μέλιτι γλυκερῷ)
context: The comparative is used figuratively of speech and affection: Nestor's voice flowing from his tongue 'sweeter than honey' (Il. 1.249), anger 'sweeter than dripping honey' (Il. 18.109), a lover addressed as 'sweeter than sweet honey' (Plautus); Lucretius' 'sweet honey of the Muses' for his verse continues the honey-sweet-speech image. Weakness: honey as the standard of sweetness is near-universal and the Aristotle anchor is plain prose description; the claim rests on both lexemes being cognate inside the same comparative construction, with Vedic showing the figure under renewal.

cognate: Gk βοῦς = Ved. gáv-/gó- = Lat. bōs (*gʷṓws); Gk ἵππος = Ved. áśva- = Lat. equus (*h₁éḱwos)
drift_or_renewal: the further members are renewed: 'small stock' Gk πρόβατα vs Ved. paśú- (*péḱu); 'man' Gk ἄνθρωπος vs Ved. púruṣa-
shared_syntax: coordinated enumeration of domestic animals headed by 'cattle' and 'horse(s)' (+ small stock + men) as representatives of all living beings: Arist. ἵππων … βοῶν … προβάτων … ἀνθρώπων … ζῴων; βοῦν … ἵππον … ζῴων ~ AVŚ 8.2 jīvati gaur aśvaḥ puruṣaḥ paśuḥ
context: In both the list stands for 'every living creature' and is tied to the root 'live' (ζῴων ~ jīvati, both *gʷeyh₃-); Cato's boues … equis lists farm animals. The Greek side is prose enumeration and the pairing of cattle and horses is natural for any herding society, so this is weak evidence for an inherited formula; the Vedic 'cows and horses' pair (góbhiḥ áśvaiḥ) is clearly formulaic on its own side.
phrase: *gʷṓwes *h₁éḱwōs (+ *péḱu, men) 'cattle and horses' as the inventory of living beings

cognate: Gk ἐγρήγορα (redupl. perfect) = Ved. jāgāra/jāgr̥- (*h₁ge-h₁gor-, *h₁ger- 'wake'); Gk ὕπνος = Ved. svápna-/svap- (*swep-/*supnó-)
drift_or_renewal: Greek often uses καθεύδω for the 'sleeping' member (renewal), keeping ἐγρηγορ- for 'waking'
shared_syntax: merism 'waking … sleeping' (Ved. jāgrad … svapann, jāgrato … svapantaḥ; Gk ὕπνοις … ἐγρηγορέναι, καθεύδοντας … ἐγρηγορότας)
context: Vedic uses the merism in confession formulas ('whatever we did, waking or sleeping'); Aristotle uses it as a philosophical contrast about perception in sleep vs waking. Both members are cognate and the 'waking' member is in both a reduplicated perfect-type formation, but the opposition is natural in any language and the Greek witness is prose with a different function; no Greek verse merism with these cognates was found (Homer only ὕπνου … ἐγείρω 'wake from sleep').

cognate: Gk κλῄω/κληΐω (from κλᾱϝίς 'bar, key') ~ Lat. claudo (*kleh₂w- 'peg, hook'); Gk θύρα(ι) = Lat. forēs (*dʰwer-/*dʰwor-, often plural 'double door')
drift_or_renewal: none in the noun; the verbs are parallel but probably separate denominal formations from the 'peg/bar' noun
shared_syntax: verb 'bar/lock' + object 'doors' (pl.): Hom. κλήϊσεν … θύρας ~ Pl. fores occlusae, Lucr. clausis foribus
context: Shutting the house doors in a domestic scene (Odysseus' hall; a lover's door in Plautus). Both lexemes are inherited and the plural 'doors' matches, but this is the ordinary way to say 'shut the door' in each language, so I treat it as at most a Greco-Italic shared usage, not a poetic formula.

cognate: Gk κύων = Lat. canis (*ḱwṓ); Gk λύκος = Lat. lupus (*wĺ̥kʷos; Lat. with Sabellic p)
shared_syntax: wolf and dogs as an opposed pair in proverbial or figurative speech: Solon (verse quoted in Ath. Pol.) κυσὶν … λύκος 'a wolf among many dogs' ~ Plautus lupi … canes 'wolves on this side, dogs on that' (a speaker trapped between two dangers); Aesch. Supp. 760 proverb λύκους κρείσσους κυνῶν 'wolves are stronger than dogs'
context: Both Solon and Plautus' speaker describe a man beset on all sides with the wolf/dog opposition used proverbially; Catullus' carrion image (canes … lupi devouring a corpse) is a separate use. Wolf and dog are an obvious natural pair, so the figure may be independent.

note: Slab dominated by Aristotle prose pivots with Cato/Plautus/Lucretius and AV partners; most bundles share only generic roots (be, do, give, bear). One strong lead (raw/human flesh, kréwh2s + h2eh3mós + h1ed-), one medium (honey-sweet comparative), four low.
